t.gol mod ii@48.0,101.2:
Gol Mod II lies in the open valleys of central Mongolia, and the first thing to know is that there is no road to it in the sense most riders mean. You reach it on tracks across the steppe, past herders' gers and grazing horses, and then the tombs appear: a field of low mounds and earthworks, and at its heart a huge square structure with a long ramp, the grave of a member of the Xiongnu elite.

The Xiongnu were the steppe empire that dominated the lands north of China from around the third century BC, the people against whom the Chinese built and extended their early walls. Their leaders were buried in deep terraced shafts under square platforms, with ramps leading down from the south, surrounded by smaller satellite graves. Gol Mod II is one of the largest of these cemeteries, and excavations by Mongolian and international teams have uncovered horse skeletons, chariots, gold and silver objects and goods from China and the West, which show how far the Xiongnu reached. Many of the tombs were robbed long ago. The neighbouring site of Gol Mod I is another large Xiongnu cemetery, and the region has deer stones and Bronze Age burials as well.

This is wild riding. The tracks are a braid of parallel ruts across grassland and gravel, firm in dry weather, slippery and boggy after rain, with river crossings that can be dangerous when the snowmelt or summer storms swell them. Navigation needs GPS and patience, since the tracks branch and fade. Summer is the only sensible season; from late autumn to spring the cold is extreme. Distances between settlements are large, and help is far away, so travelling with others is wise.

There are no towns nearby of any size. Fuel is found in sum centres, the small district towns, and in the provincial capitals such as Tsetserleg in Arkhangai; quality varies and pumps can be dry, so carry spare fuel and enough water for the day. Herders are famously hospitable, and you may be offered tea with milk and salt or a bowl of airag, fermented mare's milk, which is an acquired taste and worth acquiring.

The reward is the space. Larch forest on the north-facing slopes, grassland rolling away to the horizon, an eagle circling overhead, and two-thousand-year-old graves under a sky that seems twice the usual size. Ride slowly, camp early, and enjoy the silence.
t.deer stone monuments and related bronze:
On the open grassland of north-central Mongolia, tall grey slabs of granite stand in lines, tilted slightly towards the sky, with strange carvings on their sides. These are deer stones, and the name comes from the flying deer with long antlers that are carved on them, stylised as streams of curving lines. They were raised by Bronze Age herders about three thousand years ago, probably as memorials to important men, and some stand three or four metres tall. Mongolia has well over a thousand, more than anywhere else in the world, and the best-known groups lie around the Khangai and the northern mountains, within the broader region of the Gol Mod sites that make up this part of the map.

The carving is superb in its simplicity. The upper part of a stone often shows a sun or a face with earrings, the middle section carries a belt with tools, a knife and an axe, and the lower part has the deer, leaping with their muzzles like birds' beaks and their antlers sweeping back across the stone. Around the stones lie stone mounds called khirigsuur, and sometimes the skulls of horses buried in the surrounding circles, suggesting rituals of sacrifice. This is a landscape of ceremony, laid out on the steppe with a very deliberate hand.

Riding here is something completely different from European touring. Beyond the paved road to Tsetserleg, about thirty-five kilometres away, tracks run across the steppe in several parallel lines, and conditions depend on rain, sheep, and the last vehicle to pass. A heavy bike would struggle in sand or mud, and a small dual-sport machine with luggage is far better. Fuel is available in Tsetserleg, which is the provincial capital of Arkhangai, but not on the steppe, so carry extra and plan your range carefully. Weather changes fast, with strong winds, hail and even snow possible in summer, and nights are cold at this altitude.

The best time is from June to September, when the grass is green and the days are long. Nomadic families live in gers across the grassland, and hospitality is traditional, with salty milk tea, fermented mare's milk in summer and dried curds offered to guests. Ask permission before approaching a ger, greet with respect, and close any gate you open.
t.bronze age complex site with deer stones:
The grassland north of the Khangai range does not look like a museum, and that is its quality. Rolling green hills run off to the horizon under a vast sky, herds of horses and yaks drift across the slopes, and here and there a lone grey stone rises from the grass. A Bronze Age complex of this kind, with deer stones and burial mounds, belonged to the nomadic herders who lived on the steppe in the second and first millennia BC. Their world was horses, bows and open sky, and their monuments are simple, bold and without any written record.

The typical complex has a pattern. One or more deer stones stand in a row to the east of a group of stone mounds, while around them are low round or square enclosures and satellite mounds, each with a buried horse. The main mound, the khirigsuur, covers a central burial and is surrounded by a ring or a square of stones, sometimes with lines of small cairns radiating out like the spokes of a wheel. Archaeologists suspect the layout was linked to ideas about the sun and the cosmos. Some of these monuments are very large, and the ring of stones can be hundreds of metres in diameter.

The geography is stern and beautiful. There are no towns listed in my data for this site, so treat this as remote country where help is far away. The steppe has wide river valleys, patches of larch forest on the north-facing slopes, and sudden, sharp rainstorms. Eagles and vultures circle over the hills, and marmots whistle from their burrows, while in the evening the light turns the grass to gold.

Practically, you should plan for self-sufficiency. Carry fuel and water for the whole leg, tell someone where you are going, and keep a spare tube, tools and a paper map in case your phone fails. Tracks branch and rejoin without signs, and rivers can run high after rain. A guide or a local driver with experience is a sensible option for many travellers. Respect the monuments by not climbing on the stones or moving them, and leave no rubbish.

The deer here are made of stone and are about three thousand years old. Across the grasslands of northern Mongolia stand granite pillars carved with leaping deer, their long antlers streaming back like flames or birds' wings, with sometimes a belt, a knife or a pair of earrings scratched below. These are deer stones, raised by Bronze Age herders in the second and early first millennium BC, and Mongolia has more than a thousand of them, most in the northern provinces. Nobody is sure what they meant. One theory says they were memorials to dead warriors, another that they were altars where the soul was carried to the sky by the deer. Around them are rings and rectangles of stone and low mounds called khirigsuur, burials of the same people.

This site is near Tsetserleg, the capital of Arkhangai province, a small town of around six thousand at the foot of a wooded hill, with a pleasant museum in an old monastery building. Fuel is available in town, and it is the last reliable supply for a good distance, so fill both tank and spare can before heading out. The land beyond is steppe and valley, rolling and enormous, with the sky doing most of the work. Gers dot the hills, herds of horses and yaks drift along the rivers and eagles perch on the roadside posts.

Riding here is a matter of paved main road giving way to wide gravel tracks, river crossings and improvised routes where the main skill is route-finding. The weather can change in an hour, with summer storms, hail and a surprising chill even in July. Nights at this altitude, around a kilometre and a half above sea level, are cold. Pack warm clothes and plenty of water, and ask locals about river levels before crossing.

The nearby Orkhon Valley is a World Heritage landscape of its own, with the ruins of Karakorum, the thirteenth-century capital of the Mongol Empire, and the monastery of Erdene Zuu close by. Combined with the deer stones, it makes a rich week of history.

Traditional food is mutton and dairy: salty milk tea, hard curd, dumplings called buuz. Accept whatever you are offered in a ger. Summer is the season, with wildflowers in June and a warm blur in July.
t.hofn@64.3,-15.2:
Höfn is a fishing town that has spent decades staring at a glacier, and the glacier has finally started to answer back. It sits at the mouth of the Hornafjörður on Iceland's southeast coast, a small town of fewer than two thousand people on a low peninsula, with the vast white dome of Vatnajökull, Europe's largest ice cap by volume, filling the northern horizon. On a clear day, the tongues of ice that spill down the mountains look close enough to walk to, and at sunset they glow pink and gold. The name simply means harbour.

The town's pride is langoustine, which locals call lobster, and it appears on every menu in town from grilled skewers to soup. Boats go out for it from the harbour, and the town celebrates with a festival in summer. Behind the harbour the town has a small museum on the region's glaciers and heritage, and a short drive east, across the sands at Stokksnes, the black volcanic dunes in front of the sharp, jagged peak of Vestrahorn make some of the most dramatic photographs in Iceland. The access road is private, and a small fee is charged.

Riding the Ring Road around here is a pleasure, with long straight stretches along the coast, bridges over braided glacial rivers and views of ice and mountain. West of Höfn the road leads along the foot of the ice cap toward the Jökulsárlón glacier lagoon, about eighty kilometres away, where icebergs drift out to the sea and wash up on a black beach. East the road crosses the Almannaskarð pass, now bypassed by a tunnel, before winding along the Eastfjords. Wind is the major danger, particularly near the sands, where gusts can be violent and the sand can blast paint from the bike. Watch for sheep, and slow for single-lane bridges.

Höfn has a fuel station, a supermarket and a handful of guesthouses and restaurants, and it is the only real town for a long way in either direction, so it is the sensible place to fill up. Summer evenings are long and bright, and the town is quiet. Autumn and winter bring snow and darkness, and some roads close, so check conditions. A walk to the harbour in the late evening, as boats unload and the glacier turns red, is a peaceful way to end the day.
t.vik@63.4,-19.0:
Vík í Mýrdal is a tiny village on the south coast of Iceland with a red-roofed church on a hill, a long black beach below, and a reputation far larger than its size. A few hundred people live here, mostly in low houses below the cliffs, and the Atlantic crashes onto the sand in front of them with ceaseless force. Offshore, a group of tall basalt sea stacks called Reynisdrangar rises from the surf, and legend says they are trolls who were caught by the sun while trying to drag a ship to shore and turned to stone.

The beach at Reynisfjara, a short drive west, is one of the most photographed in the country, with black volcanic sand, a cliff of hexagonal basalt columns and a sea cave. It is also dangerous. Sneaker waves, which surge far further up the beach than the waves before, have swept visitors into the sea and caused deaths, so stay well back from the water and never turn your back on the surf. Behind the village rises the glacier Mýrdalsjökull, and under the ice lies the volcano Katla, which erupts every few decades on average and is closely watched by scientists. The last major eruption was in 1918.

For a rider, Vík is a handy and scenic stop on the Ring Road. To the west the road passes the arch of Dyrhólaey, a rocky headland where puffins nest in summer, then the waterfalls of Skógafoss and Seljalandsfoss. To the east it crosses Mýrdalssandur, a vast flat plain of black ash and sand from glacial floods, where the road runs straight for kilometres with nothing to break the wind. Crosswinds there can be strong enough to shove a bike across a lane, so grip the bars, and slow down when the gusts hit. The surface is good, but traffic is heavy in summer.

There is a fuel station in the village, along with a supermarket, a woollen mill shop and several places to eat, so it is a useful place to refuel before heading east across the long stretches to Höfn. Accommodation fills up in summer, so book ahead. Visit the beach early in the morning or in the evening light, when the crowds thin and the basalt takes on a deep glow.
t.kunming@25.0,102.7:
Kunming is called the Spring City, and the title is earned. Set at about nineteen hundred metres on the Yunnan plateau, it has mild weather almost all year, with warm days, cool nights and a long season of flowers, so that you can ride in a light jacket in January. Dian Lake, the big freshwater lake on the southern edge, spreads out under hills hazy with distance, and gulls from Siberia arrive in winter to feed on bread thrown by the crowds on the lakeside. The city itself, with more than three and a half million people, is a lively and rather modern place of tower blocks, tree-lined avenues and parks.

Kunming is a good base for the exploration of Yunnan, one of the most varied provinces in China. The Stone Forest, a maze of grey limestone pillars about ninety kilometres to the south-east, is among the best known sights. Closer to the city lies the Chengjiang fossil site, where quarries in a hillside near Fuxian Lake have yielded some of the finest fossils of the Cambrian period, about five hundred and eighteen million years old. These show soft-bodied creatures, early fish and strange arthropods, preserved in extraordinary detail, from the time when animal life burst into variety. UNESCO listed the site in 2012.

Food is a draw. Kunming is the home of crossing-the-bridge rice noodles, served as a bowl of scalding broth to which you add raw ingredients at the table, and the story behind the name involves a loyal wife who kept her husband's lunch warm under a layer of chicken fat. Yunnan is also known for its mushrooms, its cheese, a firm fried milk cake called rubing, and its coffee and tea, including Pu'er, grown in the south of the province. Flower markets spill onto the streets, and the spicy, sour flavours of the local cuisine are a pleasure.

Riders should note that foreign motorcycling in China is tightly regulated. Temporary driving permits, local licence plates and guides are often required, and rules change, so check well before you plan a trip and do not assume a normal licence will do. Fuel stations are plentiful in the city and on all main roads. The best seasons are spring and autumn, and the rainy season from June to August brings downpours and fog in the mountains. Traffic in the city is dense, with electric scooters appearing from every direction, and a slow, alert pace is wise.
t.waypoint 2@63.4,-19.1:
The south coast of Iceland has a way of making even the Ring Road feel like an expedition. Around this point you are close to Vík and the great black plain of Mýrdalssandur, a flat, dark expanse of volcanic sand laid down by glacial floods from beneath the Mýrdalsjökull ice cap. Under that ice sits Katla, one of the country's most closely watched volcanoes, and the floodwaters it can unleash are the reason the sandur looks the way it does. The road runs across it in long straight lines, with very little to break the horizon.

Riding here is a lesson in wind. The open plain has no shelter, and gusts from the Atlantic can come across at an angle that makes the bike lean without any help from you. Signs warn of crosswinds, and they mean it. Sand can blow over the tarmac in dry spells, and the coast road after rain is often slippery with fine grit. Keep a firm grip, relax your shoulders and be ready for a sudden shove when a lorry passes the other way.

The scenery rewards the effort. Vík itself is a small village with a red-roofed church on a hill above the sea, and below it lies the black beach with its basalt columns and the sea stacks of Reynisdrangar standing offshore. Legend says they were trolls turned to stone by the dawn. The waves here are powerful and unpredictable, and visitors are warned regularly to stay well back from the water. Inland, the slopes are bright with moss in summer and the glacier glints white above.

Fuel is the thing to plan. Vík has a station and a few cafes and a woollen mill shop, but the stretches on either side are long, with Kirkjubæjarklaustur to the east and Skógar and Hvolsvöllur to the west, so top up in Vík before heading on. In winter the road can close or become very difficult in wind and ice, so check the road conditions before you leave.

The best riding time is June through August, with light until late at night, though even then wet and cold days are not unusual. Pack real waterproofs and a spare layer, and take the gusts seriously.
t.vatnajokull national park dynamic nature:
Vatnajökull is the biggest ice cap in Europe by volume, a white plateau covering about eight percent of Iceland, with outlet glaciers that spill into valleys and lagoons. Beneath the ice lie volcanoes, including Grímsvötn and Bárðarbunga, that erupt from time to time, melting the ice from below and sending floods of water down the rivers. The national park that surrounds it, one of the largest in Europe, is a place where fire and ice are visibly at work on the same ground.

The nearest place with fuel is far away, at Mývatn or Egilsstaðir, and the tracks that lead here are rough mountain roads, marked with an F on the map, which cross rivers without bridges. Such routes are usually open only for a few weeks in midsummer, and the conditions change with the weather, so anyone planning to go should check road reports and travel with someone experienced.

From the Ring Road, the ice cap can be seen as a white line above the farms, and the best roadside views are on the south coast, where outlet glaciers come down almost to the sea, and icebergs float in lagoons. The mountain of Öræfajökull, rising to over two thousand metres, is the highest in Iceland. The riding, on the paved Ring Road, is wide open, with far horizons, and the wind can be fierce.

The summer months are the only practical time, and even then the weather is unpredictable, with rain, fog and cold. Carry warm and waterproof clothing, food and water, and tell someone your plan. The reward is a landscape on a primal scale, black sand, blue ice and grey sky, which makes the human world seem very small indeed.
Nakhon Si Thammarat is not on the usual list of Thai holiday places, and that is part of its charm. It is an old city on the Gulf coast of the southern peninsula, with a walled centre, a lot of history and a big temple at its heart. Wat Phra Mahathat is the biggest and most revered in the south, with a bell-shaped chedi in the Sri Lankan style that rises about thirty-seven metres, topped by a gilded spire that you can see across the rooftops. According to legend, the relics of the Buddha were brought here many centuries ago, and pilgrims have been making offerings since the city was part of the maritime trading empire of Srivijaya.

Around the main chedi, cloisters hold rows of Buddha images, and small shrines and halls crowd the courtyard. Locals come in the morning and the evening, tying cloth to the chedi, buying flowers and incense, and sitting quietly in the shade. Dress modestly, with shoulders and knees covered, and take off your shoes before going into any hall. A museum a short walk away displays regional treasures, and the city is known for nielloware, a silver craft, and for nang talung, shadow puppet theatre, that you can still find in performance.

The ride from Krabi crosses the spine of the peninsula, about two hundred kilometres, on a road that climbs through limestone and rubber plantations and drops to the flat plain on the Gulf side. It is easy, mostly straight riding, with a surface that is good by Thai standards, though lorries slow things down. Keep an eye out for the monsoon, which hits the east coast from October to January, when roads can flood and storms last for days. The dry months from February to September are safest.

Nakhon Si Thammarat is a proper city of more than a hundred and twenty thousand people, so fuel, food and hotels are easy to find. Street stalls near the temple sell khanom jeen, rice noodles with a fiery curry sauce, which is the local dish and a decent reason for lunch. Behind the city, Khao Luang is the highest mountain in southern Thailand, with rain forest and waterfalls, if you have a day to spare.
t.gerik@5.4,101.1:
Gerik sits in the far north of Perak, close to the Thai border, on the road that people call the East-West Highway, which cuts across the Malay Peninsula through some of the oldest rainforest on earth. The town itself is small and tidy, with shophouses around a main street, a market, mosques and a few modest hotels, and it exists mainly as the last proper stop before the mountains. West of it the land is flat or gently rolling. East of it the road starts to climb, runs along the vast Temenggor lake, and plunges into jungle that is said to be well over a hundred million years old.

The Belum-Temenggor forest is one of the great wild reserves of Malaysia. It shelters elephants, tigers, tapirs, gaur and the clouds of hornbills that cross the lake at dusk, and the indigenous Orang Asli, among them the Jahai, still live in and around it. You will not see much from the saddle except green walls and the occasional warning sign, but the sense of a huge, living forest on both sides is unmistakable. Bring some patience for the occasional elephant sign: they mean what they say.

The highway was built in the 1970s and early 1980s, partly for security reasons and partly to link the west coast with the poorer east, and it is one of the best rides in Peninsular Malaysia. The tarmac is good, the bends are long and rhythmic, and the climbs and descents give a real sense of travelling through mountains. It is also a road that demands attention: logging trucks and buses run it at speed, landslides sometimes close a lane after heavy rain, and the surface can have loose gravel or fallen branches on the bends. Do not ride it at night.

Gerik has fuel and a reliable stock of everything else, and that is the point of stopping here, because the highway beyond has long gaps with little in the way of services. Top the tank, check your tyres and water, and take food. The local cafés serve good rice and noodle dishes, and the fish from the lake is worth trying when you can find it. Thai influence is visible in the food, and the heat and humidity make an early start wise.
t.titiwangsa rest area@5.6,101.5:
The Titiwangsa Range is the spine of the Malay Peninsula, and this rest area sits at about 1,050 metres, near the point where the East-West Highway crosses it. In a country where most roads run through steamy lowlands, the change is striking. The air is cool and often wet, mist drifts through the trees, and moss and ferns grow thick on every trunk. The sign for the rest stop is easy to miss, but the pause is welcome after the long climb from the west, and the views over layers of forested ridges fading into blue are generous when the cloud allows.

It is a working road, so the rest area works like a roadside one: parking, toilets, a prayer room, a few stalls selling drinks and snacks, and groups of truck drivers sleeping in their cabs with the windows open. Riders come here in numbers, particularly at weekends, and it is easy to strike up a conversation with someone on a big touring bike from Kuala Lumpur or Penang. If you have a hot drink, the cold up here makes it taste better than it should.

The riding on either side of the stop is the real attraction. West of here the highway runs along the Temenggor lake and through the Belum forest, with long swinging curves and small climbs. East, it drops through a sequence of sweeping descents toward Kelantan and the east coast. The surface is generally excellent, but there are patches of damp, moss at the verges and rain squalls that arrive without warning. Keep the speed down in the mist and watch the trucks, which brake late into the bends and swing wide.

Wildlife is part of the story: gibbons call in the early morning, and you may see monkeys by the road. Elephants use the area too, and the signs warning of them are not decoration. Take warm clothing as well as rain gear, because after a long, hot day in the lowlands the damp chill at altitude can feel sharp.
t.jeli@5.7,101.8:
Jeli is a small place on the eastern side of the Malaysian peninsula, close to the border with Thailand, and it marks the end of the East-West Highway. The highway crosses the Titiwangsa mountains and comes down to a landscape of rubber plantations, small villages and rice fields in Kelantan, a state with a distinct Malay culture. There is not much in Jeli itself; the nearest sizeable town is Tanah Merah, about thirty-six kilometres away, and just across the Thai border is Su-ngai Kolok. The Jeli area is known for its Gunung Reng and hot springs.

Kelantan is regarded as the heartland of traditional Malay culture. It is known for shadow puppetry, wayang kulit, and for batik, kite-making, silverwork and the dance and music of the region. The state is conservative, and the pace of life is slower than on the west coast. Food is sweet and rich: nasi kerabu, rice coloured blue with butterfly pea flowers, served with herbs, fish and coconut, and nasi dagang, rice cooked in coconut milk. Roadside stalls sell sweet snacks and fresh coconut water.

For the rider, the highway descends from the mountains with a series of long, easy curves, through forest and then plantation. Monkeys, snakes and the odd elephant are a possibility, and the road can be wet and slippery after storms. The monsoon on the east coast, from November to February, brings heavy rain and flooding, and roads can be cut, so avoid those months. In the dry season, the heat can be strong, and early starts are advised.

Fuel is available in Jeli, but stations are less common than on the west coast, so fill up when you can. Facilities are basic, with small restaurants and some guesthouses, and cash is useful. A short distance away, the Lake Banding area and Royal Belum Park are noted for nature, birdwatching and rafting. The end of the highway offers a calm finish to the crossing, a sense of having moved from one side of the country to the other, from the busy west to the traditional east.
t.bronze age complex site with deer stones:
Out on the steppe of central Mongolia, there are stone monuments that have stood for around three thousand years. Deer stones are tall granite slabs, sometimes taller than a man, carved with images of flying deer, their long antlers sweeping back along the stone, along with belts, tools, and a sun and moon. They were erected in the Late Bronze Age, roughly between the fifteenth and seventh centuries BC, by nomadic herders who also built stone mounds and square fenced burials known as khirigsuur. The stones seem to mark graves of important people, and the deer motif has been interpreted as a vehicle for the soul to travel to the sky, though nobody knows exactly.

Herds of horses, sheep, goats and yaks dot the land, and the white felt tents, gers, stand in small clusters near water. Villages are small and far apart, and no town of any size appears in the nearby database, so you should assume that fuel and supplies are far away.

Riding in Mongolia is a different thing altogether. Paved roads connect the main towns, but off them you follow dirt tracks that braid across the grassland, and the surface changes from hardpack to sand, mud and rock without warning. River crossings can be deep after rain, and weather can turn quickly, with hail and cold wind even in July. This is serious country for experienced riders in a group, with spare fuel, a satellite beacon, and a good map. Nomadic families are hospitable, and it is customary to accept a bowl of airag, the fermented mare's milk, or salty milk tea, and offer something in return.

The best season is from June to September, when the grass is green, and the days are long, though nights can be near freezing. Spring is windy and autumn arrives early.

Treat the stones with respect: do not climb on them, do not take rubbings, and leave everything as you found it.
t.jokulsarlon@64.0,-16.2:
Jökulsárlón is a lagoon full of icebergs, and the first view of it can leave you simply standing by the bike. The ice comes from Breiðamerkurjökull, a tongue of the great Vatnajökull ice cap, which has been retreating for decades and leaving behind a deep, cold lake. The lagoon appeared in the 1930s and has grown steadily as the glacier melts back, and it is now one of the deepest lakes in Iceland, with the bottom lying a couple of hundred metres below the surface. Blocks of ice in shades of blue, white and black, striped with volcanic ash, float slowly toward a short channel where the tide carries them out to sea.

Where the water meets the Atlantic, the ice is washed up on the black sand beach, and the glittering chunks scattered across it give it the name Diamond Beach. Seals follow the icebergs through the channel, feeding on the fish that come in with the tide, and you can often watch their heads popping up beside the bridge. Arctic terns nest nearby in summer and will dive at passers-by, and great skuas cruise the shoreline. The place is so photogenic that it has appeared in James Bond films, and boat tours with amphibious vehicles or inflatable boats run in summer.

The ride along the south coast is one of Iceland's finest. The Ring Road crosses the lagoon outlet on a bridge, and between the glacier tongues and the sea lies a flat black plain, a sandur, formed by glacial meltwater, where the road runs straight for kilometres with the ice cap hanging on the horizon. It is easy riding, with a good paved surface, but wind is the constant risk, because gusts can sweep across the plain without warning and carry sand and grit, and rain can arrive from the sea in minutes. Slow down on the one-lane bridges, and watch for sheep.

There is limited fuel in the immediate area, so plan your fills carefully. Höfn, about eighty kilometres to the east, is the main town with a full range of services, and the glacier area at Skaftafell to the west has more limited provisions. A small cafe by the lagoon sells soup and coffee, which is welcome in the cold air. Summer brings long days and the midnight sun, but crowds are heavy in the middle of the day, so early morning or evening visits are better, when the ice glows in a softer light.
t.landmannalaugar junction@64.0,-19.1:
Landmannalaugar looks as if someone has spilled a paint box over the mountains. The hills around the camp are made of rhyolite, a volcanic rock that weathers in shades of pink, yellow, green, blue and purple, and in the evening, with the low sun on them, they glow like embers. Beside the camp is a black lava field, the Laugahraun, and a stream of warm water runs through it from hot springs, where trekkers sit in a natural pool after a long day on the trail.

This is the start of the Laugavegur trail, one of the best-known walks in Iceland, which runs for fifty-odd kilometres to Þórsmörk, and in summer the camp is crowded with hikers, tents and buses. The huts are run by the Icelandic Touring Association, and the whole place has the feel of an outpost, with a small shop, toilets and a car park full of big four-wheel-drive vehicles. The volcano Hekla, which has erupted many times in recorded history, stands to the south-west.

The roads to Landmannalaugar are mountain tracks, not highways. Most visitors arrive on the F208 or by the track from Route 26, both of which involve loose gravel, lava rock and several river crossings, some of them deep, and they are officially open only in summer, usually from late June, when the snow melts. Conditions change from day to day, so check the road authority's website for closures and river depths before setting off, and think hard about whether your machine, your tyres and your nerve are up to it. It is a hard ride, not a casual one.

Carry food, water and warm clothes, since the weather in the highlands can turn from sunshine to sleet in an hour, and always tell someone your route.
t.nyidalur@64.7,-18.1:
Nýidalur is a mountain hut in the middle of nowhere, at about eight hundred metres, on the long, empty route of Sprengisandur that runs through the centre of Iceland. It sits in a green valley called Jökuldalur between two great ice caps, Hofsjökull to the west and Vatnajökull to the east, with the peak of Tungnafellsjökull rising nearby, and the whole landscape around it is a vast desert of black gravel and lava, with only a few patches of moss and grass. It is about as remote as you can get in Europe.

The hut is run by the Icelandic Touring Association, and has a warden in summer, a campsite and basic rooms for walkers and riders. It is a lifeline for those crossing the highland, and a fine place to stop for the night, with a stream running by and an enormous sky above. In the evening, the light is long and low, and the silence is complete. The road to the hut is a rough track, but it is an unforgettable place to rest, and the people you meet here are likely to be good company.

Sprengisandur was once one of the main routes across the island, used by farmers and travellers in the days before cars, and many people are said to have disappeared in the desert, as the weather can turn very fast. Folklore has it that outlaws hid in the interior, and ghosts and trolls are said to haunt it. Today, the route is open only in summer, usually from early July to September, and crossing it needs a sturdy machine, good preparation and careful attention to the rivers.

The hut sells nothing, so bring food, water and a stove, and keep your phone charged, though coverage is patchy. If the weather turns bad, it is better to stay put and wait than to push on.
t.gol mod i@48.3,101.9:
Gol Mod sits in the open grass country of central Mongolia, where the land rolls away in long folds beneath an enormous sky and the only landmarks are herders' white felt tents, gers, and the occasional lonely mountain. The place is known to archaeologists for its cemeteries of the Xiongnu, the nomadic confederation that dominated the steppe two thousand years ago and rivalled Han China, and the graves of their elite are found in valleys like this.

Xiongnu tombs have a typical look: a square mound on the surface with a ramp, over a deep pit that holds a wooden chamber and coffin. Some contain silks, lacquer, jade, bronze mirrors and horse gear, evidence of trade and tribute with China and other lands. Researchers have found that these nomads were far from simple, building complex burials and keeping contacts across Eurasia. The ride's other theme, the deer stones, belongs to a still earlier age of the Bronze Age: tall standing slabs carved with flying deer, belts and weapons, set up about three thousand years ago.

Riding here is real adventure. Surfaces vary from paved main roads to wide, braided dirt tracks across the grass, and rivers must be forded. Weather swings from hot sun to hail within an hour, and winter is brutally cold, so summer, from June to August, is the time. Navigation needs GPS and local knowledge, since there are few signs and many tracks, and herds of horses, yaks and sheep share the way. Herder families usually welcome travellers with salty milk tea and dried curd, and it is polite to accept.

There are no towns close by to rely on, so carry fuel, spares, food and water for the stage. The nearest services are in aimag centres such as Bulgan or Tsetserleg, and Ulaanbaatar lies several hours away. Dogs at gers can be fierce, so stay near your bike until called off. The reward is space, silence and the sense of riding through a landscape where history is written lightly on the grass.
t.penang@5.4,100.3:
Penang is an island of the Strait of Malacca that behaves like a small country, with its own food, language habits and pride. The British East India Company's Francis Light took possession of it in 1786 and founded George Town as a free port, and the city quickly filled with Chinese, Indian, Malay, Arab, Armenian and European traders. The grid of narrow streets with shophouses, clan houses, temples, churches and mosques, many within a few steps of one another, earned UNESCO listing together with Melaka in 2008.

The architecture is the pleasure, with pastel-painted shophouses and five-foot walkways, the sea-front clan jetties built on stilts over the water, and the ornate Khoo Kongsi clan house, with its carved roofs and courtyards. Street art by Lithuanian-born artist Ernest Zacharevic, painted on walls in 2012, gave the city a second fame. Kek Lok Si, a hillside Buddhist temple above Air Itam, has a pagoda and a huge statue of Kuan Yin, and Penang Hill, reached by funicular railway, is cool and misty.

Hawker food is the true attraction. Char kway teow, noodles stir-fried over fierce heat with prawns and egg, assam laksa in sour fish broth, and nasi kandar, rice with curries ladled over it, are among the dishes people cross oceans for. Eat at open-air hawker centres and kopitiams, coffee shops where aunties serve strong coffee with condensed milk.

On two wheels, the island is rewarding. A coastal road circuits it, passing Batu Ferringhi's beaches, fishing villages and the national park at Teluk Bahang, with rolling hills and views. Two long bridges link the island to the mainland, the older one opened in 1985 and a second, longer one in 2014, and the ride across the first gives a fine panorama. Traffic is heavy at rush hour, and the heat and humidity are constant, with rain showers from April to October. Fuel is easy. The Lenggong Valley, about a hundred and fifty kilometres to the south-east, is a world away in mood.
t.bukit kepala gajah@5.1,101.0:
Bukit Kepala Gajah, Elephant Head Hill, is one of the limestone outcrops in the Lenggong Valley of Perak, a landscape where the Malay Peninsula's earliest people left their tools in the soil. The valley lies along the Perak river in the north of the state, among steep green karst hills, rubber plantations and small villages, and UNESCO inscribed it in 2012 as a site of archaeological heritage, giving it a reputation as one of the oldest in Southeast Asia.

The most famous finds are stone tools found at Kota Tampan, which are dated to about seventy thousand years ago and lie beneath a layer of volcanic ash from the eruption of Toba in Sumatra, one of the largest eruptions in history. That finding helped scholars argue that early people survived the catastrophe in this region. Other caves nearby yielded Perak Man, a skeleton about eleven thousand years old, the oldest complete human skeleton found in Malaysia, unearthed in a cave in 1991.

The hills themselves are strange and beautiful: sheer white cliffs hung with vines, caves with bats and swiftlets, and green forest at the foot. Hornbills fly over, and monkeys watch from the trees. The roads are narrow and winding, partly shaded by rubber trees, with farm vehicles and slow lorries, and the surface is decent but can be slick after rain. Heat and humidity are constant, with afternoon storms in the monsoon seasons.

Lenggong, the small town, has fuel, a few food stalls and a museum that displays the finds, and the old royal town of Kuala Kangsar lies to the south with its golden-domed Ubudiah Mosque. Eat Perak specialities at roadside stalls, such as river fish and sweet tea. Check what is open before visiting, since archaeological sites are often fenced and need permission, and keep to marked paths. The best light is early morning, when mist hangs between the hills.
t.bukit gua harimau@5.1,101.0:
Gua Harimau means Tiger Cave, and the name hints at the stories that surround this limestone hill in the Lenggong Valley. The cave was excavated by archaeologists in the first decade of this century, and what they found was remarkable: a large number of human burials from the Neolithic and later periods, buried with pottery, tools and ornaments, which helped show that people lived and buried their dead here over thousands of years.

Researchers studying the skeletons learned about the health, diet and ancestry of ancient people in the peninsula, since DNA and isotope work can reveal where they came from. Some skeletons were buried in a crouched position, others laid out with grave goods that included bronze and iron, showing contact with wider trading networks. Findings like these are part of why Lenggong was listed by UNESCO, along with its tools and Perak Man.

The hill rises sharply from the plain, and the cave is entered through a wide opening halfway up. The forest around it is humid and loud with insects, and monsoon rain makes the paths slippery. The limestone is fretted by water into sharp pinnacles, and bats stream out at dusk. Wildlife is not hard to see, with squirrels, macaques, and a chorus of frogs after rain.

Visits should be planned locally. Access is usually controlled, so ask at the Lenggong archaeological gallery about guides and permission, and wear boots, long sleeves and repellent. The nearest town for fuel is Lenggong, and Gerik, on the East-West Highway, lies further north, with the forest of the Belum area beyond. A meal of rice with fish curry and a glass of iced tea in a village stall completes the visit. Be respectful, since graves are involved, and do not touch or remove anything, however small a potsherd or bone fragment may look lying loose in the soil. Local people know these hills well and are usually glad to explain what they know, so a few polite questions and a small purchase at a stall go a long way toward making the visit welcome. The valley rewards slow riders more than fast ones.
t.bukit jawa@5.1,101.0:
Bukit Jawa is one of the smaller hills of the Lenggong Valley, and like its neighbours it carries traces of very old human presence under tropical growth. The valley sits in northern Perak where the river Perak winds through a plain framed by limestone ridges, and the archaeology here suggests that people came to this region repeatedly, drawn by the river, the caves and the stone suitable for tools.

For a visitor, the interest is as much in the landscape as in any single find. The karst hills rise abruptly from flat fields, with white cliffs and forested tops, and the old rubber and oil palm plantations that cover the lowlands give the area its green, orderly look. Paddy fields and small orchards surround Malay villages, with wooden houses on stilts. Lenggong is also close to Lake Raban, a pleasant stretch of water used for fishing.

Riding in the valley is gentle and rural. Back roads, lined with rubber trees and shaded by large rain trees, pass fish ponds, mosques and shops selling kuih, sweet cakes. Traffic is light, and the main hazards are slow lorries carrying logs or palm fruit, stray dogs and sudden rain. April to October is the drier half, and November to March brings heavier rain. Mornings are cool and clear, and the afternoon heat is heavy.

Fuel is available in Lenggong town and Gerik, and it is sensible to fill the tank before wandering the back lanes. The Lenggong Archaeological Gallery gives context for the hills, with displays of tools and skeletons, and staff can tell you which sites are open. Stop at a roadside stall for fried bananas or a coconut, and take time to look at the cliff faces, which hide caves and ancient stories. Treat the fenced sites with care. If the sky darkens in the afternoon, take shelter early, because tropical storms here arrive suddenly, drop a great deal of water in minutes and leave the narrow lanes slick with red mud and fallen leaves. Evening brings a soft, cooler light across the paddies, and the cliffs turn pale gold, which makes the late ride back to town one of the nicest parts of the day.
t.kjolur highland road point 2@64.9,-19.6:
Hveravellir is a geothermal field in the middle of Iceland, a small patch of boiling springs, steaming vents and mineral crusts in the heart of a vast, cold desert. It lies about halfway along the Kjölur road, in a hollow between Langjökull and Hofsjökull, and arriving here after hours of gravel feels like finding a lit window in a dark house. The ground steams, the pools are turquoise and green and orange, and the smell of sulphur drifts across the plain.

The ride here is demanding but rewarding. The Kjölur track is gravel all the way, with washboard sections, loose stones and the occasional deep patch of sand, and wind that can knock a bike sideways. Allow plenty of time and keep your speed down, particularly on the corners, where loose gravel gathers. The road is open only in summer, usually from June to September, and weather can change fast, with snow possible even in July.

There is a human story here, too. In the eighteenth century an outlaw named Eyvindur and his wife Halla are said to have lived at Hveravellir, hiding from the authorities after he was convicted of theft. They survived the winters by using the hot springs for cooking and warmth, and the ruins of their little shelter, built from stones and turf, can still be seen near the springs. They became folk heroes, and Halla was reportedly a fierce and resourceful woman, who gave birth to a child here, in the middle of nowhere.

The nature is surreal. The field contains a wide variety of hot springs, with colours caused by minerals and microbes, and a small natural pool where you can bathe if you like, when the temperature is right. The surrounding land is a mix of lava, sand and moss, with no trees for hundreds of kilometres. The silence is profound.

A hut and a simple campsite serve walkers and riders in summer, and a warden is often present, but do not expect more than basic facilities. Bring warm clothing, and take care near the springs, where the ground can be thin and the water scalding.
t.sprengisandur highland road point 2@64.0:
Nobody believes Landmannalaugar until they see it. The mountains are not grey or brown but streaked with yellow, pink, green, blue and a deep rusty red, as if a giant had spilled a paintbox down the slopes, and the colours come from rhyolite, a volcanic rock rich in silica and stained by minerals. Beside them lie black lava fields and a steaming river, and the whole scene looks painted rather than made. The place is part of the Fjallabak nature reserve, a wild corner of the southern highlands.

Getting here is an adventure in its own right. The roads that lead in are gravel mountain tracks with river crossings, some of them deep enough to need care and a bike with decent ground clearance, and they open only in summer, depending on snow, usually from about June. Conditions change with rain and meltwater, and the crossings can be harder in the afternoon when glacial streams rise. Look at the road authority's reports, ride with company if you can, and do not be too proud to turn back.

Landmannalaugar is the starting point of the famous Laugavegur trek, which runs about fifty-five kilometres south to Þórsmörk, and in July the hut here is crowded with walkers. A natural hot spring runs into a cold stream, creating a bathing spot where the temperature depends on exactly where you sit, and riders with tired shoulders will find it a blessing. The name means the people's pools, a nod to the long history of travellers who rested here on the way across the highlands.

Nature is sparse but spectacular. The ground is covered with moss and lichen, and the lava of the Laugahraun field is jagged and black. Torfajökull, a huge volcanic complex, sits behind the camp, with steam rising from the hillsides in many places. The air is cold and carries a faint smell of sulphur.

Facilities are limited to a mountain hut, a campsite and a seasonal cafe, so bring your own supplies and expect no phone signal. Choose a stable weather window, and give the place at least an hour for a walk among the colours.
t.sprengisandur highland road point 3@64.7:
Nýidalur sits at around eight hundred metres in a stony hollow beneath the Tungnafellsjökull glacier, and it feels as remote as any place in Europe. A pair of huts run by the Iceland Touring Association stand in a landscape of black gravel and pale sky, with the nearest farm hours away in any direction. It is roughly the midpoint of the Sprengisandur highland route, and the arrival here after hours on a rough track is both a relief and a quiet marvel.

The road is demanding. The Sprengisandur is a long gravel track across the high desert between the icecaps, with corrugations, loose gravel, sand patches and rivers that can be crossed only with care, and it opens for a short season in summer, normally from late June or July. Weather can be savage, with wind, rain and even snow at any time, and visibility can drop quickly. Bikes need to be well prepared, riders need experience, and it is wise to travel in company and tell someone your plans.

The name Sprengisandur comes from a verb meaning to burst, and the sense is of horses ridden to the point of collapse in the long, waterless crossing. For centuries this was one of the few routes between north and south, used by travellers and outlaws, and folk tales are full of ghosts, trolls and lost men. The old cairns that mark the way are still there. The desert itself is a plateau of volcanic sand and rock, shaped by wind and ice, with the great ice cap of Vatnajökull to the south-east.

Nature is minimal but enthralling. A few hardy plants grow in sheltered gullies, and the colours of the rock and sky dominate. Geese nest in some of the wetter places, and a few hardy sheep wander, but there is little else. The silence is extraordinary, with only the wind and the occasional trickle of meltwater.

The huts provide basic shelter and a warden in season, but do not rely on supplies. Carry water, food, warm clothing and the means to call for help. Take time to look around: this is as wild as it gets.
t.malaysia east west highway point 2@5.4,1:
Gerik is the last town in Perak before the East-West Highway heads off into the jungle, and it has the feel of a frontier: a single main street, a few petrol stations, shops selling everything from fishing nets to motorcycle parts, and roadside restaurants serving nasi campur and roti canai to truckers and travellers. The town sits in a broad valley surrounded by forested hills, and the Perak river flows nearby. Thailand is less than forty kilometres to the north, and the border town of Betong is the nearest large settlement.

The highway that starts here, linking Gerik with Jeli in Kelantan, was built in the 1970s and early 1980s through some of the wildest country in the peninsula. It was a strategic as much as an economic project: the area was a stronghold of communist insurgents, and the road was meant to bring government control to the border region. Construction was dangerous, with workers and soldiers killed in attacks, and it was completed only after years of effort. Today, the road is a scenic route through dense rainforest, and the area is peaceful.

Just east of Gerik lies Temenggor Lake, a huge reservoir created by a hydroelectric dam, with forested islands and inlets stretching for kilometres. The lake is surrounded by the Belum-Temenggor forest complex, one of the oldest rainforests in the world, home to elephants, tigers, tapirs, hornbills and many other species. Boat trips from Banding Island, where the highway crosses the lake on a long bridge, take visitors into the forest to see waterfalls, Orang Asli villages and, with luck, wildlife.

For riders, Gerik is the place to fill up and eat before the long stretch through the jungle to Jeli, where services are few. The highway itself is well paved, with long sweeping bends and steep climbs, and it is popular with Malaysian riders at weekends. Watch out for trucks, which are slow on the climbs and fast on the descents, and for elephants, which sometimes cross the road, especially at night. Signs warn of elephant crossings, and they are not a joke. Ride in daylight, carry water, and expect rain in the afternoon.
t.malaysia east west highway point 3@5.6,1:
Around 1,050 metres up, the East-West Highway crosses the spine of the peninsula, the Titiwangsa Range, which divides Perak from Kelantan and the west coast from the east. Up here the forest is dense and green, the air is cool and damp, and the views stretch over endless forested ridges with no sign of human activity, apart from the road itself. It is one of the most remote places in Peninsular Malaysia, and it feels it: no towns, no villages, just jungle and the occasional viewpoint where people stop to look.

The forest here is part of the Belum-Temenggor complex, a vast area of rainforest that extends across the border into Thailand. It is ancient, having survived the ice ages, and it is extraordinarily rich in species: all ten species of hornbills found in Malaysia live here, along with Asian elephants, Malayan tigers, tapirs, sun bears and many others. Rafflesia, the parasitic plant whose genus produces the largest single flowers in the world, blooms in the forest at certain times of the year, and local guides can sometimes take visitors to see it.

The road at this height is all curves and gradients, a series of long climbs and descents through the forest, with good asphalt and wide lanes. It is a joy to ride, but there are hazards: fog, which can reduce visibility to a few metres; rain, which can be torrential and turns the road slippery; and wildlife, especially elephants, which use the road to move between parts of the forest. Signs warn of elephant crossings, and there have been collisions, mostly at night. There are also landslides after heavy rain, so watch for debris.

There are no services here, apart from the occasional roadside stall selling drinks and snacks. The nearest fuel is in Gerik, behind you on the Perak side, or Jeli, ahead on the Kelantan side, and the Thai town of Betong is the nearest large settlement, though not reachable directly from here. Make sure you have enough fuel and water before you start the crossing, and plan to do it in daylight. A stop at one of the viewpoints, with the forest stretching away into the mist, is the best reward for the effort.
t.malaysia east west highway point 4@5.7,1:
Coming down off the Titiwangsa on the Kelantan side, the jungle slowly loosens its grip. The road drops towards the town of Jeli, rubber and oil palm plantations begin to replace the forest, and kampung houses on stilts appear among fruit trees. Here the highway meets the east coast world: a different dialect, a different cuisine, a more conservative culture, and in Kelantan the weekend falls on Friday and Saturday rather than Saturday and Sunday, which can catch out anyone planning around shop hours.

Near Jeli lies the Pergau Dam, a hydroelectric project built in the 1990s that became famous far beyond Malaysia. Its funding was tied up in a British political scandal over aid and arms deals, and the affair led to a landmark court case in London. Today the lake behind the dam is quiet and green, surrounded by forest, and the road around it makes a pleasant detour. Jeli also has natural hot springs, where locals boil eggs in the water and soak their feet, and the countryside around has waterfalls in the forest.

Kelantan is one of the most distinctive states in Malaysia, with a strong Malay identity and a rich tradition of crafts and performance: kite making and flying, top spinning, batik and songket weaving, and shadow puppetry. The food is a reason to linger. Nasi kerabu, rice tinted blue with butterfly-pea flowers and served with herbs, fish and coconut, is the signature dish, along with nasi dagang and grilled chicken with a sweet, spicy sauce. Roadside stalls in Jeli serve these dishes for a few ringgit.

The highway on this side has long descents with sweeping bends, then flattens out as it approaches the plains. Watch for trucks, motorbikes and livestock, and for elephants in the forest sections, especially at dusk. Jeli has fuel, food and basic accommodation, and Tanah Merah, about thirty-five kilometres further east, is a larger town with more services. From there, the road continues to Kota Bharu and the coast. The monsoon season, from November to February, brings heavy rains and flooding to Kelantan, so March to October is the riding season here.
